name: Combining Qualitative and Quantitative Data
title: Combining Qualitative and Quantitative Data
answer: Combining qualitative and quantitative data is the practice of bringing interview transcripts, field notes, open survey answers and other text or media together with counts, scores and measurements in one study. It sits inside mixed methods research, where the aim is usually to explain a pattern, to check whether a finding holds across sources, or to let one strand of evidence raise questions the other can answer. The unit of work is the study design rather than a single dataset, so the topic covers sampling, sequencing and the point at which the two kinds of material are brought into contact.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Combining qualitative and quantitative data is the practice of bringing interview transcripts, field notes, open survey answers and other text or media together with counts, scores and measurements in one study. It sits inside mixed methods research, where the aim is usually to explain a pattern, to check whether a finding holds across sources, or to let one strand of evidence raise questions the other can answer. The unit of work is the study design rather than a single dataset, so the topic covers sampling, sequencing and the point at which the two kinds of material are brought into contact.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The quantitative side typically runs on statistical software and tabular stores, while the qualitative side runs on coding tools that hold transcripts, audio, video and annotations. Common choices include R, Python and SPSS for the numbers, and NVivo, ATLAS.ti, MAXQDA or Dedoose for the text, with spreadsheets and relational databases acting as the join point between them. Where the two are merged, the practical infrastructure is often a shared codebook or a case identifier that lets a coded excerpt be matched to a row of survey or sensor data.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work usually follows one of a few recognised designs: convergent, where both strands are gathered in parallel and merged at interpretation, explanatory sequential, where numbers come first and interviews follow, or exploratory sequential, where interviews inform the design of an instrument. Analysis proceeds by coding qualitative material into themes, running the quantitative analysis separately, then joining the two through a matrix, a joint display or a narrative that sets themes against variables. Integration is the hard part, and it is done deliberately at the design, methods or interpretation stage rather than left to the discussion section.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Mixed methods studies inherit the ethics of both traditions, which means consent that covers re-use of quotes alongside data protection for the numeric files, and care over whether small qualitative samples could identify a person once linked to survey responses. Provenance matters because a theme is only as good as the coding behind it, so audit trails, intercoder agreement checks and versioned codebooks are standard practice. On this site, content links to the original paper rather than to a search tool, which keeps the chain from claim back to source intact.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward more automated support for the qualitative half, with language models used to draft codes, suggest themes and align excerpts to variables, always under human review. That raises the prospect of larger qualitative datasets being analysed at a scale that makes integration with quantitative data routine rather than exceptional. The open questions are how to keep transparency when a model sits between the transcript and the theme, and how journals and reviewers will treat machine-assisted coding in mixed methods work.
